text: Among 109 subjects who had undergone cardiac surgery under ECC, the authors recorded 50 (45 p. 100) who suffered from shivering during the postoperative recovery period. Comparing the series of patients who shivered, with that of the subjects who did not shiver, the authors demonstrate in the first case, an increase in cellular metabolism, the cardiac index, heart rate, central venous pressure, and cardiac work. They subsequently note the appearance of mixed acidosis and an increase in the lactate-pyruvate ratio. Certain patients, in whom the cardiac output did not match the metabolic demand sufficiently, experienced a decrease in arterio-venous oxygen difference. Blood loss was also increased, along with coagulation time, which showed a less intense heparin rebound. The study of the drugs used during anesthesia revealed that the patients who had received chlorpromazine, as the antipsychotic, a medication with anticholinergic properties, had a significantly higher frequency of shivering compared to those who had received droperidol. The placement of the patient at the end of the intervention on a heating mattress, combined with the administration of chlorpromazine during anesthesia, prevented the appearance of shivering.
